papers.title: The landscape of AI speech generation and deepfake detection
papers.abstract: Synthetic speech has reached a level of naturalness that can deceive listeners into believing they are hearing natural speech. This opens up the possibility of using synthetic speech deepfakes to mislead both human listeners and automated systems. One response to this threat is to attempt to automatically detect deepfakes. This report offers the reader a self-contained overview of the landscape of synthetic speech generation and speech deepfake detection. It is intended to be accessible to a general audience and therefore includes brief histories of both fields, definitions of all acronyms, a glossary of technical terms, and an extensive bibliography for those who wish to read more.

papers.title: When Sounds Turn Heads: Recovering Event Timing That Audio LLMs Fail to Say
papers.abstract: Audio LLMs can know when a queried sound occurs but fail to say it. We find a few attention heads that track the queried sound: they shift when the query changes, follow the sound when it moves, and removing or blocking them often hurts the model's timestamps. Yet the answer does not express what they track. Intervals read directly from these heads outperform the model's original answer and recover events that its timestamps miss. To bring this timing into the answer, we introduce head-guided decoding, which needs no training. It keeps the model's decision on whether the sound is present and rescores its candidate timestamps with a prior from these heads. Heads selected on development data transfer unchanged to new recordings and free-text queries, where head-guided decoding improves the timestamps of three audio LLMs, scores above their head readout on every benchmark, and, in most settings, outperforms random-head guidance. On recordings released after the models were trained, head-guided decoding raises mIoU from 0.07-0.36 to 0.48-0.56. These results suggest that poor temporal answers in audio LLMs partly reflect a failure to say rather than to hear, and that the model's own attention can close part of this gap.

papers.title: From Attention to Semantics: Detecting and Mitigating Sound Event Hallucinations in Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) excel at diverse audio tasks, yet remain prone to hallucinating sound events absent from the input. Prior work links such hallucinations to insufficient audio attention. However, we find that real and hallucinated events can receive comparable audio attention mass while attending to different audio positions. To examine whether the attended representations support the generated events, we adapt LatentLens to retrieve neighboring contextualized text representations. The retrieved contexts reveal semantic support for real events, but a semantic mismatch between hallucinated events and their attended audio representations. Directly masking the corresponding audio regions can suppress hallucinated events at the cost of real content. We are motivated by these findings to introduce an explainable and training-free detect-then-mitigate framework for effectively hallucination detection and mitigation that aggregates semantic support and applies differential audio masking to protect regions associated with events predicted to be supported. Extensive experiments on three LALMs and two datasets demonstrate that our method significantly improves hallucination detection and hallucination mitigation performance.

papers.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
papers.abstract: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

# HeartMuLa-oss-3B ONNX

ONNX builds of [HeartMuLa-oss-3B](https://huggingface.co/HeartMuLa/HeartMuLa-oss-3B), made by Moonbox for on-device use with ONNX Runtime (CPU, CUDA, DirectML). Each
precision is one folder holding the graphs and a small Python `pipeline.py` that does the rest (features, prompt,
sampling loop, codec windows); what the graphs take and return is under *How to run*.

## How to run

HeartMuLa-oss-3B (a 3B music language model that turns lyrics and style tags into a song, with the HeartCodec audio
codec; 48 kHz stereo) as ONNX graphs plus `pipeline.py`, a numpy runtime that reproduces the official heartlib
`HeartMuLaGenPipeline` (@1647883) around them.

- `decoder.onnx`: the 28-layer Llama-3.2-3B backbone (onnxruntime-genai's model builder): `inputs_embeds`
  [2, S, 3072] (classifier-free guidance: row 0 conditional, row 1 unconditional), `attention_mask`,
  `past_key_values.{0..27}.key / .value` [2, 8, past, 128] -> `hidden_states` (after the final norm) and `present.*`.
- `embed.onnx`: `tokens` [B, S, 9] (8 codebooks + the text token), `tokens_mask` [B, S, 9], `uncond` [B] -> `h`
  [B, S, 3072]: the masked sum of audio and text embeddings (the unconditional text embedding on CFG's second row).
- `head.onnx`: `hidden` [B, 3072] -> codebook-0 logits [B, 8197].
- `depth.onnx`: the 3-layer depth decoder: `hidden` [B, 3072], the codebooks so far `codes` [B, J] and `j` [1] (= J)
  -> logits [B, 8197] of codebook J. No cache: a frame has 8 positions.
- `codec_cond.onnx`: codes [1, 8, N] -> the flow's condition [1, 2N, 512] (RVQ lookup, projection, nearest x2).
- `estimator.onnx`: HeartCodec's flow-matching transformer, static [2, 744, 1024] (latent, in-context latent,
  condition; the codec always decodes 29.76 s windows with guidance), `t` [2] -> velocity [2, 744, 256].
- `scalar_dec.onnx`: the scalar codec's decoder: latent [B, 128, T] -> audio [B, 1, 1920 T].
- `muq.npy`: the reference-audio slot of the prompt (heartlib has no reference audio yet: `muq_linear(0)` for the
  conditional row, the unconditional text embedding for the other).

The backbone's fp16 build overflows on the unconditional row, whose prompt is one embedding repeated (cosine 0.13 to
float32). In `decoder.onnx` the residual stream is therefore divided by 8: `v_proj`, `up_proj` and the input
embeddings by 8, and the RMSNorm epsilon by 64. RMSNorm ignores its input's scale, so the hidden states are unchanged
(cosine 0.99999 to float32 on both rows).

`pipeline.py` does the rest in numpy:
- the prompt: lower-cased `<tag>tags</tag>` and lyrics, each wrapped in the begin / end-of-text tokens, with the
  empty reference-audio slot between them (`tokenizer.json`, `tokenizers`);
- the frame loop: guidance 1.5 on every codebook, top-k 50 at temperature 1.0, until a codebook says end of audio
  or the length runs out;
- the codec: 29.76 s windows with hop 80 / 93. Each window takes the previous one's last latents as its in-context
  start and runs 10 Euler steps with guidance 1.25. Each window goes through the scalar decoder, and the windows are
  joined by linear cross-fades.

It needs numpy, onnxruntime-gpu (or onnxruntime), tokenizers and soundfile:

```bash
python int8/pipeline.py out.wav --tags "pop, upbeat, female vocal, piano, drums" --lyrics lyrics.txt --seconds 30 --cuda
```

```python
import sys, soundfile as sf
sys.path.insert(0, "int8")
import pipeline
m = pipeline.HeartMuLa("int8", "cuda")
song, sr = m("pop, upbeat, female vocal", "[verse]\nwalking down the street in the morning light", seconds=30, seed=0)
sf.write("song.wav", song.T, sr)                     # 48 kHz stereo
```

Sampling uses numpy's generator, so a seed gives the same song every run here, not the same song as PyTorch with that
seed. The pipeline frees the LM's sessions before the codec and the flow before the scalar decoder. On Windows, give
CUDA sessions the run option `memory.enable_memory_arena_shrinkage` = `gpu:0`, as `pipeline.py` does. Every input
length differs, so ONNX Runtime's GPU arena otherwise keeps growing.

`tokenizer.json` (from HeartMuLa/HeartMuLaGen) is byte-identical to Meta's Llama 3.2 tokenizer; HeartMuLa labels it
Apache-2.0. If you treat it as Llama Materials, the Llama 3.2 Community License applies to it ("Built with Llama").

**Precisions.** `fp16/`: the backbone fp16 (builder, residual scaled as above), every other graph fp16 weights with
fp32 inputs / outputs. `int8/`: the backbone 8-bit MatMulNBits (block 32), the embedding tables int8 per row; the head,
depth decoder and codec as in `fp16/`. `int4/` (LM below threshold, experimental): the backbone 4-bit MatMulNBits
(block 32), the rest as `int8/`. Two things stay fp16 in the int folders:
- The codec: weight-only int8 put it at 22.8 dB from the original (its scalar decoder rounds `9 z`, which amplifies
  small changes).
- The depth decoder and head: they run 7 times a frame, and weight-only int8 dequantizes their weights on each run
  (2.9 frames/s against 5.9).

Speed on an RTX 3080 Laptop GPU (16 GB), `int8/`: the LM makes 5.9 frames/s (12.5 frames are 1 s of audio), and the
codec decodes 10 s of audio in 10 s. No bf16 build:
fp16 passes.

**Benchmark.** Sampled songs differ from run to run, so every build scores the same codes. The original (heartlib in
bfloat16 on CUDA, seed 0, CFG 1.5) generated 12 s for 2 prompts: "pop, upbeat, female vocal, piano, drums" and "folk,
acoustic guitar, male vocal, calm", each with two lines of lyrics, 151 frames each. Each build then predicts every
frame teacher-forced. Codebook 0 comes from the backbone; codebooks 1-7 come from the depth decoder fed the true
earlier codes, with guidance as in generation. The scores are KL(float32 || build) of the guided distributions and
top-1 agreement with float32. The float32 reference is the original's modules in float32 on the same codes (the
backbone streamed layer by layer). Pass (music LM): mean KL at most 0.01 nats and agreement at least 90 %. The codec
decoded the first song with the original's own random draws; the score is SNR against the original's float32 output.
Pass (first measurement): at least 30 dB.

## How to run

**Powered by Stability AI.** Stable Audio 3 Medium makes instrumental music, sound beds and sound effects from a
description: 44.1 kHz stereo, up to 380 seconds, in 8 steps. It has no lyrics input.

Each folder is a whole pipeline for `mlx_model.py`, the one-file MLX runtime that sits in the folder (mlx, numpy,
sentencepiece; no PyTorch):

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `dit.safetensors` | the diffusion transformer (1.45 B parameters); its attention and feed-forward layers MLX affine-quantized to 8, 6 or 4 bits, group size 64, the rest float16 |
| `decoder.safetensors` | the SAME-L decoder, latents to audio (float32); the same file in every folder |
| `text_encoder.safetensors`, `tokenizer.model` | the encoder half of T5Gemma b-b-ul2 (float16) and its vocabulary; the same in every folder |
| `conditioner.safetensors` | the prompt padding embedding and the seconds embedder |
| `config.json`, `mlx_model.py` | sizes and quantization; the runtime |

```bash
pip install mlx numpy sentencepiece soundfile
hf download moonbox-dev/stable-audio-3-medium-MLX --include "8bit/*" --local-dir sa3
```

```python
import sys, soundfile as sf
sys.path.insert(0, "sa3/8bit")
from mlx_model import Pipeline

pipe = Pipeline("sa3/8bit")          # one part in memory at a time: text encoder, transformer, decoder
audio, info = pipe.generate("Warm lofi hip hop with dusty drums, mellow Rhodes piano and deep bass, 85 BPM",
                            seconds=30, seed=11)
sf.write("lofi.wav", audio.T, pipe.sample_rate)
```

On an Apple M5 a 20-second clip takes about 3 seconds and 4 GB of memory. The model code is
[mlx-audio](https://github.com/Blaizzy/mlx-audio)'s `stable_audio_3` (MIT); the weights are Stability AI's own MLX
export ([stabilityai/stable-audio-3-optimized](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-audio-3-optimized)), renamed
and, for the transformer, quantized. There is no fp16 folder here: that is Stability's export itself.

**How they were checked.** Each build against the fp16 export in the same runtime from the *same* noise: 4 clips
(lofi, orchestral, folk, rain; 12-47 s, seed 11). "First step" is the relative error of the transformer's first
output; "log-mel" the mean difference of the two clips' log-mel spectrograms; CLAP
(`laion/clap-htsat-unfused`) scores a clip against the fp16 clip and against its prompt. For scale, a *different seed*
of the fp16 build scores log-mel 3.8-10.2 dB and CLAP 0.90-0.95 against the first, and the same file scores CLAP
0.98-0.99 against itself. Pass: first step <= 0.10 and log-mel <= 2.0 dB on every clip. The export itself wasn't
compared with a PyTorch run.

| Precision | Size (transformer) | First step | Log-mel vs fp16 | CLAP vs fp16 / vs prompt | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp16 export | 5.18 GB (2.91) | reference | - | 0.98-0.99 / 0.61 | Stability's export, not in this repository |
| `8bit/` | 3.90 GB (1.63) | 0.008-0.025 | 0.26-0.82 dB | 0.972-0.990 / 0.61 | passes: the same clip |
| `6bit/` | 3.57 GB (1.29) | 0.023-0.088 | 0.60-1.65 dB | 0.943-0.988 / 0.61 | passes: small differences |
| `4bit/` | 3.23 GB (0.95) | 0.13-0.37 | 2.1-3.9 dB | 0.967-0.986 / 0.62 | **below threshold, experimental**: a different rendition of the prompt, same character |

The decoder's output can pass full scale on loud material; `generate()` clips it to [-1, 1] (`clip=False` returns it
as decoded).

# Stable Audio 3 Optimized

> **Note:** This repository contains experimental checkpoints optimised for acceleration on specific hardware. For standard checkpoints, please use [Stable Audio 3 Medium](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-audio-3-medium) instead.

Please note: For commercial use, please refer to [https://stability.ai/license](https://stability.ai/license)

## Model Description
`Stable Audio 3` is a family of fast latent diffusion models (small, medium, large) for variable length audio generation and editing. Since our models can generate several minutes of audio,
variable-length generations are key to avoid the cost of producing full-length generations for short
sounds. We also support inpainting, enabling targeted audio editing and the continuation of short
recordings. Our latent diffusion models operate on top of a novel semantic-acoustic autoencoder that
projects audio into a compact latent space, enabling efficient diffusion-based generation while preserving audio fidelity and encouraging semantic structure in the latent. Finally, we run adversarial
post-training to both accelerate inference and improve generation quality, reducing the number of inference steps while improving fidelity and prompt adherence. Stable Audio 3 models are trained on
licensed and Creative Commons data to generate music and sounds in less than a 2s on an H200 GPU
and less than a few seconds on a MacBook Pro M4. We release the weights of small and medium,
that can run on consumer-grade hardware, together with their training and inference pipeline.

## Usage

This model can be used with:
1. the [`stable-audio-3`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3) inference and fine-tuning library
2. the [`stable-audio-tools`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-tools) research library


### Using with `stable-audio-3`
```python
from stable_audio_3 import StableAudioModel

model = StableAudioModel.from_pretrained("medium")
audio = model.generate(
    prompt=(
        "House music that encapsulates the feeling of being at a festival "
        "in the sunny weather with all your friends 124 BPM"
    ),
    duration=180
)
```

### Using with `stable-audio-tools`
```python
import torch
import torchaudio
from einops import rearrange
from stable_audio_tools import get_pretrained_model
from stable_audio_tools.inference.generation import generate_diffusion_cond_inpaint

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
if device == "cuda":
  model_half = True

# Download model
model, model_config = get_pretrained_model("stabilityai/stable-audio-3-medium")
sample_rate = model_config["sample_rate"]
sample_size = model_config["sample_size"]

model = model.to(device)
if model_half:
  model = model.to(torch.float16)
# Set up text and timing conditioning
conditioning = [{
    "prompt": (
        "A dream-like Synthpop instrumental that would accompany "
        "a dream-sequence in a surrealist movie 120 BPM"
    ),
    "seconds_total": 380
}]

# Generate stereo audio
output = generate_diffusion_cond_inpaint(
    model,
    steps=8,
    cfg_scale=1.0,
    conditioning=conditioning,
    sample_size=sample_size,
    sampler_type="pingpong",
    device=device
)

# Rearrange audio batch to a single sequence
output = rearrange(output, "b d n -> d (b n)")

# Peak normalize, clip, convert to int16, and save to file
output = output.to(torch.float32).div(torch.max(torch.abs(output))).clamp(-1, 1).mul(32767).to(torch.int16).cpu()
torchaudio.save("output.wav", output, sample_rate)
```


### Optimized CPU runtime (TFLite / LiteRT)

Portable CPU builds live in [`optimized/tflite`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3/tree/main/optimized/tflite). The SAME autoencoder ships as static **rung** `.tflite` codecs at `tflite/same-{s,l}/{enc,dec}_{fp32,w8a8}.tflite` — one weight-shared file per encoder/decoder that dispatches a fixed-size subgraph per length, keeping RAM flat and avoiding a chunk-size knob. They require **`ai_edge_litert>=2.2.0`** and are driven by the `RungEncoder` / `RungDecoder` runtime in that directory (`w8a8` is the default; `fp32` is the bit-exact reference). The earlier dynamic-length codecs are preserved under `tflite/same-*/legacy/`.

### Runtime LoRA on TensorRT (NVIDIA)

`dit_fp16_lora.trt` is a DiT with a **runtime low-rank branch** on each adapted linear. All
three DiTs have one:

| engine | DiT | targets | size |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-m/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | medium, 24 × 1536 | 229 | 2.96 GB |
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-sm-music/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | small-music, 20 × 1024 | 193 | 0.95 GB |
| `tensorRT/sm_90/sa3-sm-sfx/dit_fp16_lora.trt` | small-sfx, 20 × 1024 | 193 | 0.95 GB |

A TensorRT plan has its weights compiled in, so an adapter cannot be merged into it the way
the CPU runtime does; these engines instead take the adapter as *network inputs* — `A`, `Bt`
and a per-output-row rescale `P` are fed in like activations, with the rank as a dynamic
dimension — and compute `y = W₀·x·(1+P) + Btᵀ·(srow ⊙ (A·x))`.

So loading an adapter is a buffer write rather than a rebuild: adapters swap in milliseconds,
several stack by concatenating along the rank axis (up to a total of 512), and `srow` gives
each one its own strength. `P` is what DoRA needs — its per-row magnitude rescale is a change
to the *base* path that no low-rank branch can express.

The branch costs a flat few ms per step, so its relative price depends on which DiT it is
attached to. On medium that is +13% at L=4096 and +37% at 1292; on the small DiTs the same
absolute cost lands on a base step about 2.7× cheaper, so at stack rank 16 on an H200 it is
+34% at L=4096, +60% at 1292 and +83% at 323. It is paid even with an *empty* stack — in fact
rank 1 is the most expensive configuration, since TensorRT picks a worse tactic below rank 8
— so use `dit_fp16.trt` until an adapter is actually wanted. That matters more on the small
DiTs than on medium.

**Adapters are not portable between the three DiTs**: different depth and width, so a medium
adapter will not load against a small engine.

**sm_90 only**; other architectures build locally in ~5–8 min, since TensorRT bakes the GPU
architecture into the plan. The runtime, the adapter row-norm baking step and the layer maps
all live in
[`optimized/tensorRT/scripts/lora`](https://github.com/Stability-AI/stable-audio-3/tree/main/optimized/tensorRT/scripts/lora)
— this repository holds only the compiled plans.

first block 23 / 8 dB; RTF 0.66 (CUDA) | ## How to run **License note.** DiffRhythm 2's own weights (the DiT, the embeddings, the decoder) are Apache-2.0. `style_text.onnx` is converted from **OpenMuQ/MuQ-MuLan-large, which is CC-BY-NC-4.0: non-commercial use only**. It holds MuQ-MuLan's text tower: XLM-RoBERTa-base (MIT) plus MuLan's own layers. DiffRhythm 2 needs a MuQ-MuLan style embedding (512-d) to generate, so commercial use needs another source of that embedding. DiffRhythm 2 (ASLP-lab / Xiaomi: a 1.1B block flow-matching model for full songs from lyrics and a style prompt; 48 kHz) as ONNX graphs plus `pipeline.py`, a numpy runtime that reproduces the official `CFM.sample_block_cache` + `decode_audio` (github.com/xiaomi-research/diffrhythm2 @13a7b09) around them. - `dit.onnx`: the 16-layer DiT: `x` [B, N, 512] (embedded lyrics or latents), `time` [B, N], `position_ids` [B, N], `style` [B, 512], `past_key_values.{0..15}.key / .value` [B, 16, P, 128] -> `velocity` [B, N, 64] and the call's own `present.*` [B, 16, N, 128]. - `text_embed.onnx` (lyrics tokens [B, L] -> [B, L, 512]) and `latent_embed.onnx` (latents [B, N, 64] -> [B, N, 512]). - `decoder.onnx`: the BigVGAN decoder, one 20-frame chunk: latent [B, 64, 20] -> 48 kHz audio [B, 1, 192000]. - `style_text.onnx`: MuQ-MuLan's text embedding of the style prompt: `input_ids`, `attention_mask` [1, T] -> `style` [1, 512] (`style_tokenizer/` is its XLM-RoBERTa tokenizer). `pipeline.py` does the rest in numpy: - the lyrics, then 2-second blocks of 10 latent frames; - per block, 16 Euler steps over linspace(0, 1, 16) with classifier-free guidance 2.0 against a zero style and zero lyrics, both kept in the batch; - the KV cache: the lyrics' keys and values (time -1) and every finished block's (time 1); - the end of the song where a latent frame reaches the all-ones end frame; - the decoder's 20-frame chunks with 5 frames of overlap. Lyrics come in as the official frontend's phoneme ids: diffrhythm2's `g2p` (pypinyin, a polyphone BERT, espeak). It isn't ported here; `pipeline.lyrics_to_tokens(lyrics, repo)` calls it from a checkout of the official repository. On Windows, `espeakng-loader` supplies espeak, and `pyopenjtalk-plus` replaces pyopenjtalk. Output is mono; the official script's fake stereo isn't included. ```python import sys, soundfile as sf sys.path.insert(0, "fp16") import pipeline m = pipeline.DiffRhythm2("fp16", "cuda") tokens = pipeline.lyrics_to_tokens("[verse]\nwalking down the street in the morning light", "diffrhythm2") song, sr = m(tokens, "pop, upbeat, female vocal, piano, drums", seconds=60, seed=0) # 48 kHz mono sf.write("song.wav", song, sr) ``` Sampling uses numpy's generator, so a seed gives the same song every run here, not the same song as PyTorch with that seed. On Windows, give CUDA sessions the run option `memory.enable_memory_arena_shrinkage` = `gpu:0`, as `pipeline.py` does. Every input length differs, so ONNX Runtime's GPU arena otherwise keeps growing. **Precisions.** `fp16/`: every graph fp16 weights with fp32 inputs / outputs. `int8/`: weight-only int8 (per output channel; the lyrics embedding table per row). `int4/`: the DiT's MatMuls 4-bit MatMulNBits (block 32), the rest as `int8/`. No bf16 build: fp16 passes. **Benchmark.** The block sampler is chaotic: even the original's own fp16 run drifts from its float32 run block by block, with the same noise. In the first block it is 56 dB from float32; in the tenth, 3 dB. So songs aren't compared sample by sample. Each build is judged the way the original is, at generation level. Two songs (style "pop, upbeat, female vocal, piano, drums" with English lyrics, and "folk, acoustic guitar, male vocal, calm" with Chinese lyrics) are generated with seeds 0-3, 20 s each. Each song is scored by MuQ-MuLan's audio-text similarity to its style prompt; MuQ-MuLan is the model's own style encoder. The original is the official sampler and decoder in fp16 on CUDA, as inference.py runs on a GPU. Pass: per song, mean similarity at most 0.03 below the original's. Real-time factor (processing time / audio time) on an RTX 3080 Laptop GPU (16 GB), sampling and decoding. | | MuLan similarity, song 1 / song 2 (4 seeds) | first block vs float32, same noise | Real-time factor | |---|---|---|---| | original (PyTorch fp16, CUDA) | 0.513 / 0.547 | 56 / 54 dB | 0.70 | | ONNX graphs in float32 (not published) | - | 64 / 62 dB | - | | `fp16/` (CUDA) | 0.532 / 0.561 | 37 / 35 dB | 0.38 | | `int8/` (CUDA) | 0.582 / 0.551 | 41 / 36 dB | 0.95 | | `int4/` (CUDA) | 0.612 / 0.548 | 23 / 8 dB | 0.66 | Each similarity is the mean over 4 seeds; the seeds alone move it by several hundredths, so a build above the original isn't better, just within the spread. Graphs checked against the original modules before the benchmark (largest absolute difference, float32): DiT 1.7e-6 of 2.1 (past 113 positions), lyrics embedding 0, latent embedding 7e-7, decoder 1.3e-6, style text 1.2e-7 against `MuQMuLan(texts=...)`. ## How these were made From [DiffRhythm 2](https://huggingface.co/ASLP-lab/DiffRhythm2) at revision `9aa15742e4`. The graphs were exported from the original PyTorch modules with torch.onnx (opset 17 / 18) and checked against them; language-model decoders were built with onnxruntime-genai's model builder (inputs_embeds in, KV cache in and out). Weight-only quantization: int8 is a per-output-channel int8 weight behind DequantizeLinear (or 8-bit MatMulNBits in the LM), int4 is ONNX Runtime's MatMulNBits (block 32). Each card above says which precision every graph uses. Every precision was benchmarked against the original before upload (the pass criteria are under *How to run*), and the `sha256` column above is what the files must hash to. ## License Apache-2.0. These files are a derivative of the original model and carry its license: it is copied in this repository, and it governs your use of these files. # Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE

**Das Full-Duplex-Sprachmodell für Deutsch. Saturn hört zu und spricht gleichzeitig, so wie Menschen miteinander reden.**

### ▶ [Live-Demo: hardani.de/saturn](https://hardani.de/saturn/)

[Deutsch](#deutsch) · [English](#english) · [Schnellstart / Quickstart](#schnellstart--quickstart) · [Dateien / Files](#dateien--files)

---

## Deutsch

Saturn führt natürliche, flüssige Gespräche auf Deutsch. Es übernimmt das Wort, sobald Sie aufhören zu sprechen, spricht trotz Hintergrundgeräuschen weiter, reagiert auf „mhm“ und „ja“, ohne den Faden zu verlieren, und lässt sich jederzeit unterbrechen. Alle 133 ms hört Saturn einen Takt Ihrer Stimme und erzeugt einen Takt eigener Sprache. Dazwischen gibt es keine Spracherkennung, keine Textkette und keine separate Sprachausgabe.

### Highlights

- **Echtes Full Duplex mit 7,5 Hz.** Zuhören und Sprechen passieren im selben Rechenschritt: Unterbrechen, Rückmeldungen, Überlappungen und Pausen entstehen ganz natürlich.
- **Für Deutsch gemacht.** Trainiert auf umfangreichen deutschen Gesprächsdaten. Saturn spricht lockeres Alltagsdeutsch mit natürlicher Betonung, Füllwörtern und Timing.
- **Stabiler Sprecherwechsel.** Saturn übernimmt in 100 % der Testfälle das Wort (Basismodell: 40 %), antwortet nach rund einer halben Sekunde und lässt keine Gesprächsrunde unbeantwortet.
- **Robust im echten Raum.** Nach Störungen wie Fernseher oder Nebengesprächen nimmt Saturn das Gespräch in 100 % der Testfälle wieder auf.
- **Stärkerer deutscher Sprachkern.** Der Text-Loss auf deutschem Text sinkt gegenüber dem Basismodell von 4,73 auf 2,09.
- **Jede Stimme, jeder Charakter.** Eine Referenzaufnahme von 3 bis 30 Sekunden legt die Stimme fest. Eine kurze Charakterkarte bestimmt Persona, Situation, Beziehung und wie oft Saturn Rückmeldungen gibt.
- **Schnell.** Der GGUF-Build rechnet den Sprachkern in rund 6,5 ms pro Takt und den ganzen Takt in rund 11 ms auf einer einzelnen GPU, mehr als 12-mal schneller als Echtzeit.

### Einsatzgebiete

- **NPCs und interaktive Spielfiguren.** Figuren, mit denen man wirklich sprechen, sie unterbrechen und mit ihnen scherzen kann, in Echtzeit.
- **Gesprächspartner und Begleiter.** Entspannter, freundlicher Smalltalk, der sich wie ein Gespräch mit einem Menschen anfühlt.
- **Deutsch üben.** Ein geduldiger Gesprächspartner für Lernende, der natürliches Alltagsdeutsch spricht.
- **Interaktive Geschichten und Hörspiele.** Figuren mit eigener Stimme und Persönlichkeit, die live auf die Zuhörenden reagieren.
- **Avatare, Terminals und soziale Roboter.** Natürliche Sprachinteraktion für verkörperte Agenten.
- **Forschung.** Eine starke deutsche Grundlage für Full-Duplex-Dialog, Sprecherwechsel und Rückmeldeverhalten.

|---|---|---|
| Übernimmt das Wort, wenn Sie aufhören ↑ | 0,40 | **1,00** |
| Antwortzeit nach Ihrem Sprechende ↓ | 1,03 s | **0,50 s** |
| Spricht nach einem „mhm“ weiter ↑ | 0,20 | **1,00** |
| Nimmt das Gespräch nach Störung wieder auf ↑ | 0,00 | **1,00** |
| Verstummt bei Hintergrundgeräuschen ↓ | 1,00 | **0,20** |
| Unbeantwortete Runden in Gesprächen ↓ | 7 / 26 | **0 / 26** |
| Sprachmodell-Verlust auf deutschem Text ↓ | 4,73 | **2,09** |

Laufzeit (GGUF bf16, eine RTX PRO 6000, geteilte GPU): Sprachkern rund 6,5 ms, ganzer Takt rund 11 ms pro 133-ms-Takt, mehr als 12-mal Echtzeit.

### Training

Saturn ist eine Weiterentwicklung von Haru-4B. Das Training kombiniert:

- **Full-Duplex-Gesprächssprache** mit Schwerpunkt Deutsch, getrennten Sprecherkanälen, wortgenau ausgerichtetem Textstrom und laufender Anreicherung mit echten Hintergrundgeräuschen (Fernseher, Nebengespräche, Rückmeldungen).
- **Charakterkarten-Konditionierung**, damit Persona, Situation und Anrede über das ganze Gespräch erhalten bleiben.
- **Wissensdestillation** von einem starken Textmodell auf deutschem Text für einen reicheren deutschen Sprachkern.
- **Text-Wiederholung** mit deutschen Frage-Antwort- und Logikdaten, damit die Sprachfähigkeit beim Sprechenlernen erhalten bleibt.
- **Stimm- und Takt-Anker**, damit Tonkopf, Stimmklonen und Taktverhalten des Basismodells vollständig erhalten bleiben.

Verwendete öffentliche Datensätze sind unter anderem Seamless Interaction und Expresso, CALLHOME (Deutsch, Englisch, Spanisch), MagicData-Gesprächssprache, OpenAssistant OASST2, GermanQuAD, XQuAD, MLQA, Belebele, MKQA, der Aya-Datensatz und die deutsche Wikipedia.

---

## English

**A German-first full-duplex spoken dialogue model. Saturn listens and speaks at the same time, the way people talk to each other.** Try it live: **[hardani.de/saturn](https://hardani.de/saturn/)**

Saturn holds natural, flowing conversations in German. It takes the turn the moment you stop, keeps talking through background noise, reacts to "mhm" and "ja" without losing its train of thought, and lets you cut in at any time. Every 133 ms it hears one frame of your voice and produces one frame of its own speech, with no speech recognizer, text pipeline or separate TTS in between.

### Highlights

- **True full duplex at 7.5 Hz.** Barge-in, backchannels, overlaps and pauses come out naturally.
- **German-first.** Colloquial, everyday German with natural prosody, fillers and timing.
- **Stable turn-taking.** Takes the turn in 100 % of the test cases (base model: 40 %), answers in about half a second and leaves no turn unanswered.
- **Robust in real rooms.** Picks the conversation back up after TV or overlapping voices in 100 % of the test cases.
- **Stronger German language core.** German text LM loss drops from 4.73 to 2.09.
- **Any voice, any character.** A 3–30 s reference clip sets the voice, a short character card sets persona, situation, relationship and backchannel frequency.
- **Fast.** GGUF build: ~6.5 ms per frame for the language core, ~11 ms for the whole frame, more than 12× faster than real time on a single GPU.

### Use cases

Game NPCs and interactive characters · companions and chat partners · German conversation practice · interactive stories and audio drama · avatars, kiosks and social robots · full-duplex dialogue research.

### Results

![Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE vs. base model](assets/saturn-vergleich.png)

| Metric | Base | **Saturn** |
|---|---|---|
| Takes the turn after the user stops ↑ | 0.40 | **1.00** |
| Response time after the user stops ↓ | 1.03 s | **0.50 s** |
| Keeps talking after a "mhm" backchannel ↑ | 0.20 | **1.00** |
| Resumes after background interruption ↑ | 0.00 | **1.00** |
| Falls silent under background noise ↓ | 1.00 | **0.20** |
| Unanswered turns in multi-turn conversations ↓ | 7 / 26 | **0 / 26** |
| German text LM loss ↓ | 4.73 | **2.09** |

### Training

Fine-tuned from Haru-4B on German-heavy full-duplex conversational speech with real background-audio augmentation, character-card conditioning, knowledge distillation on German text, German QA and reasoning rehearsal, and voice and timing anchors that preserve the base model's audio head, voice cloning and frame timing. Public datasets used include Seamless Interaction and Expresso, CALLHOME (German, English, Spanish), MagicData conversational speech, OpenAssistant OASST2, GermanQuAD, XQuAD, MLQA, Belebele, MKQA, the Aya dataset and German Wikipedia.

## Schnellstart / Quickstart

**Haru-Runtime (PyTorch, ~12 GB GPU):**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru && cd Haru
pip install -e ./haru
python -m haru.server --hf-repo keyvan-ai/Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE --language de --temperature 0.5
# lokal / local copy: python -m haru.server --model /path/to/Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE --language de --temperature 0.5
```

<http://localhost:8998> öffnen, Stimme wählen, Charakterkarte auf Deutsch schreiben und lossprechen. Kabelgebundene Kopfhörer sorgen für die geringste Latenz. / Open the page, pick a voice clip, write a German character card and start talking. Wired headphones give the lowest latency.

**Python:**

```python
from haru import DuplexConfig, DuplexSession, HaruModel
from haru.audio import load_audio, prepare_reference
from haru.prompt import card_templates, render_card

model = HaruModel.from_pretrained("keyvan-ai/Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE")
card = render_card({"name": "Lena", "gender": "female", "backchannel": "mid",
                    "persona": "Lena ist 30, arbeitet als Grafikdesignerin und erzählt mit Humor.",
                    "relationship": "Die beiden sind befreundet und duzen sich.",
                    "situation": "Ein entspanntes Gespräch am Abend über die Woche."},
                   card_templates()["templates"]["de"])
voice = prepare_reference(load_audio("voice.wav"))
session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice, config=DuplexConfig(temperature=0.5, top_k=25))
frame = session.start()
while not frame.done:
    frame = session.step(user_audio)   # 3200 Samples bei 24 kHz rein, frame.audio: 3200 Samples raus
```

**GGUF-Runtime (llama.cpp, ~11 GB GPU):**

```bash
hf download keyvan-ai/Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE --include "gguf/*" "runtime/*" --local-dir Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE
cd Saturn-Duplex-5B-DE
# llama.cpp und runtime/libsaturn_kern.so nach runtime/BUILD.md bauen, haru-Paket installieren (siehe oben)
python runtime/beispiel_duplex.py frage.wav gespraech.wav \
    --gguf gguf/saturn-duplex-5b-de-bf16.gguf --companion gguf/saturn-companion.safetensors --reference stimme.wav
```

`gespraech.wav` ist Stereo: links die Person, rechts Saturn. In Python ersetzt `SaturnModell` aus `runtime/saturn_gguf.py` das `HaruModel`:

```python
from saturn_gguf import SaturnModell

model = SaturnModell("gguf/saturn-duplex-5b-de-bf16.gguf", "gguf/saturn-companion.safetensors")
session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice, config=DuplexConfig(temperature=0.5, top_k=25))
```

Empfohlene Einstellungen / recommended sampling: Temperatur 0,5 · top-k 25 · Guidance 1,5.

# Haru-4B MLP GPTQ W4A16 (G32)

**Full-duplex Haru with 3.02 GiB less peak VRAM.** Haru keeps listening while it speaks. We measured the saving against BF16 on one RTX 6000 Ada with a single active vLLM-Omni call. This build is for voice agents and robots that need GPU headroom for other models.

> **7.28 GB** of weights · **7.5 Hz** duplex audio · **GPTQ W4A16** with Marlin in the Ada pilot

Try both sides of the audio stream in your browser. [Haru Live GPTQ on ZeroGPU](https://huggingface.co/spaces/Twu31/haru-gptq-zerogpu-lab)

## Why this build

We quantized the 96 backbone MLP projections with symmetric GPTQ W4A16, group size 32, and exported packed INT4 in `compressed-tensors` format. We verified all 926 other tensors against the BF16 checkpoint byte for byte, including the audio projections, MeanFlow head, VibeVoice codec, attention, Gated DeltaNet and tied text embedding. [Base checkpoint revision](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B/tree/8d6e83bcd3701a76fc27a764965665da1df7da78)

Calibration ran through eight duplex sessions. BF16 Haru heard Mandarin meeting speech and generated its own audio during the replay. We collected **3,474 live MLP input positions** after prompt and voice-reference prefill, covering about 7.1 minutes of input including gaps. GPTQ used 5% damping. [AISHELL-4, CC BY-SA 4.0](https://www.openslr.org/111/)

## Quick start

Use an isolated CUDA environment with `hf` and `git`. The Ada pilot used vLLM 0.33.0 and the native vLLM-Omni integration with the included patch, which sets the vendored codec window kernel to two Triton pipeline stages. [Native Haru integration](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/pull/10301) · [Ada patch](haru-ada.patch) · [Haru deployment profile](haru.yaml)

```bash
hf download Twu31/Haru-4B-MLP-GPTQ-W4A16-G32-Lab --local-dir ./haru-gptq
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni.git
git -C vllm-omni checkout 8f6c00733081d9bbfb50810621de048da3fc540d
git -C vllm-omni apply "$PWD/haru-gptq/haru-ada.patch"
VLLM_OMNI_TARGET_DEVICE=cuda python -m pip install "vllm==0.33.0" ./vllm-omni "websockets>=14"
vllm serve ./haru-gptq --omni --deploy-config ./haru-gptq/haru.yaml
```

Connect a duplex client to `/v1/realtime?duplex=1`. Configure the session with `session.update`, then send base64-encoded 24 kHz mono PCM float32 LE in 3,200-sample frames with `input_audio_buffer.append`. Send silence as the first frame. The server returns PCM16 audio and transcript deltas. [Haru duplex client protocol](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/blob/8f6c00733081d9bbfb50810621de048da3fc540d/recipes/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B-H200.md#supported-model-contract)

## Native vLLM-Omni pilot

Both checkpoints ran on one RTX 6000 Ada with a single session and a 512 MiB KV cache. We replayed two recorded Mandarin scenarios in real time with three seeds each.

| Metric | BF16 | GPTQ W4A16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Weight payload | 10.54 GB | 7.28 GB |
| Sampled peak device-memory increase | 12.57 GiB | 9.56 GiB |
| Median per-call p95, loopback audio-frame exchange | 20.11 ms | 16.76 ms |
| Median time from user speech end to model audio | 533 ms | 933 ms |
| Interruption trials with a valid speaking trigger | 2/3 | 3/3 |
| Median time to acoustic pause, valid trials | 267 ms | 267 ms |

Device memory was sampled with `nvidia-smi` every 0.4 seconds and reported above the idle baseline. Loopback timing measures a send-to-output exchange, excluding the first frame of each call. GPTQ added 400 ms to the median time from the end of user speech to model audio in this pilot. Acoustic timings use a two-frame energy threshold on a 133 ms grid. A zero can include model audio already playing at the boundary. Physical 12 GB GPU tests and broader Mandarin turn-taking evaluation are pending. Our local BF16 test on vLLM 0.34 with Model Runner V2 stopped on an error during duplex warm-up.

## ZeroGPU demo

The browser demo uses Haru's PyTorch duplex session and a Triton kernel that reads the same packed INT4 projections. A Chromium test with a simulated microphone verified concurrent audio input and output. On the ZeroGPU Blackwell partition, per-call p95 was 73–74 ms for model compute and 400–453 ms for the client audio-frame round trip on our test connection.

On two matched Mandarin interruption tests, the first pause came at **933 and 667 ms** with speech input and **800 and 667 ms** with silence. These tests verified overlapping speech. Faster yielding to interruptions remains unverified.

On 64 live BF16 activation positions from one held-out Mandarin call, the pooled relative L2 error was **5.11%** for GPTQ and **13.99%** for round-to-nearest using the same group size and scales. The audit sampled the middle 128 output channels of each of the 96 MLP projections.

This checkpoint modifies Haru-4B by quantizing its MLP weights and updating its model configuration to describe the packed format. The checkpoint is distributed under Apache 2.0. [Haru-4B by higurashi-ai](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B) · [LICENSE](LICENSE)

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - es - pt - de - fr - zh - ja - ru - ko pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: - speech - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - haru --- # Haru-4B [Code](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru) · [Technical blog](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b/) · [Technical blog (Japanese)](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b-ja/) Haru-4B is a low-latency and multilingual full-duplex continuous spoken dialogue foundation model: it listens and speaks at the same time, the way people do on a phone call. It is a pretrained base model, released for research. - **Native full-duplex at 7.5 Hz.** Every 133 ms the model takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of its own audio and text. User audio, model audio and model text are summed into a single position of the language model, so listening and speaking never wait for each other. - **Continuous audio, one sampling step.** Audio is a 64-dimensional latent per frame. A small MLP head with MeanFlow sampling produces it in one step from the language model's hidden state; there is no separate audio transformer and there are no discrete audio tokens. - **Character and voice control.** A text card sets the character, a short reference clip sets the voice. - **Multilingual.** English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Korean.

## Usage The code is at : a PyTorch implementation with a web demo, an MLX implementation with a native macOS app, and a plugin for serving with vLLM-Omni. With an NVIDIA GPU (about 12 GB of memory): ```bash git clone https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru && cd Haru pip install -e ./haru python -m haru.server --hf-repo higurashi-ai/Haru-4B ``` Open , pick a character, give the model a voice, and talk. For low latency, we recommend wired headphones and a wired microphone. Bluetooth devices add 100 ms or more. **Bring your own voice.** Haru ships without voice clips. Upload or record a clip of the voice the model should speak with: one speaker, 3 seconds to 3 minutes, clean speech. Only use voices you have the right to use. ```python from haru import DuplexSession, HaruModel from haru.audio import load_audio, prepare_reference model = HaruModel.from_pretrained("higurashi-ai/Haru-4B") voice = prepare_reference(load_audio("voice.wav")) session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice) frame = session.start() # the model's first 133 ms: frame.audio, frame.text while not frame.done: frame = session.step(user_audio) # 3200 samples at 24 kHz in, 3200 out ``` The system prompt is a character card with a fixed layout; the repository's README shows how to build one. ## Files | File | Contents | | --- | --- | | `model.safetensors` | All weights (bfloat16): `lm.*` language model, `model_audio_proj.*` / `user_audio_proj.*` audio input projections, `head.*` MeanFlow head, `codec.*` audio codec | | `config.json` | Model configuration | | `tokenizer.json` | Text tokenizer | ## Architecture | Part | Details | | --- | --- | | Language model | Qwen3.5-4B text backbone, 32 layers, hidden size 2560 | | Audio codec | VibeVoice acoustic tokenizer, causal, 24 kHz, 3200 samples per latent | | Audio head | 4-layer MLP, MeanFlow, 1 sampling step, guidance scale 1 to 2 (default 1.5) | | Frame rate | 7.5 Hz | ## Limitations Haru-4B is a pretrained base model, released for research. It holds a natural conversation, but it is not a reliable source of facts and does not follow instructions the way an assistant does. It can imitate the voice of a reference clip; only use voices you have the right to use. ## License The weights are released under the Apache License 2.0.

# tropa-voice-mini — ONNX int8

ONNX export with int8 weights of
[wasitaigeneratedcom/ai-voice-detector-small](https://huggingface.co/wasitaigeneratedcom/ai-voice-detector-small)
(tropa-voice-mini by wasitaigenerated.com), revision `4858b4064b1f8530def904e6340d2780ad847160`,
Apache-2.0. Backbone: [facebook/wav2vec2-xls-r-300m](https://huggingface.co/facebook/wav2vec2-xls-r-300m)
(Apache-2.0) with an SLS attention head. All credit for the model and its training goes to the
original authors; this repository only changes the file format so it runs with ONNX Runtime on CPU
without PyTorch.

## Conversion

- `torch.onnx.export`, opset 17, dynamic batch and length.
- `onnxruntime.quantization.quantize_dynamic`, int8 weights, **MatMul only**, per-channel.
  Default dynamic quantization of all ops drifted noticeably; MatMul-only stays close to fp32
  (mean |Δlogit| 0.04 over 638 test windows).
- Size: 357 MB (fp32 original: 1.26 GB).

## Usage

- Input `wav`: float32 `[batch, samples]`, mono, 16 kHz, one window of up to 6 s (96,000 samples).
  The graph normalizes each window itself (zero mean, unit variance).
- Output `logit`: float32 `[batch]`, AI-voice logit for the window.
- Calibrated probability, from the original `serving_head.json`:
  `p = sigmoid(1.4467909565475723 * logit + 1.3162840910986644)`.
  Original thresholds: p ≥ 0.819 (1% false-positive rate), p ≥ 0.961 (0.5%).

```python
import numpy as np, onnxruntime as ort
s = ort.InferenceSession("model_int8.onnx", providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
logit = s.run(None, {"wav": window[None].astype(np.float32)})[0][0]
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(1.4467909565475723 * logit + 1.3162840910986644)))
```

## Limitations

Not an independent accuracy claim. Our own small check (98 synthetic clips incl. ElevenLabs v3/v4,
14 real YouTube interviews/lectures) is promising but far too small to establish a false-positive
rate. See the original model card for the authors' benchmarks and limitations.

Apache-2.0, same as the original model (see `LICENSE`).
